slides.title: Large range does not mean exact detail
keyPoints: Precision limits significant information
Range limits magnitude
Choose an error budget for the application
slides.narration: A measuring instrument may need to describe very large distances without distinguishing every tiny fraction at that scale. Floating-point formats make a similar tradeoff: an exponent supplies a wide range, while a fixed number of significant bits limits detail. These are separate properties. A format can represent a huge power of two exactly while failing to distinguish nearby consecutive integers. That makes it a poor default for exact ticket identifiers or byte counts, even though those numbers fit within its magnitude range. Begin with the application's acceptable error and exactness requirements. The type is useful when its approximation model fits those requirements, not merely because it can display many digits.
actions: Ask learners to distinguish maximum magnitude from spacing between nearby values.

question.prompt: Why is floating point a risky choice for exact identifiers?
question.answer: Its finite precision can map distinct large integer identifiers to the same representable value.

slides.title: A floating value has interacting fields
keyPoints: Sign selects direction
Exponent scales the significand
Special exponent patterns change the interpretation
slides.narration: For a normal binary floating-point value, think of a signed significant number multiplied by a power of two. The stored exponent is biased so the format can encode negative and positive scale factors. In binary32, a normal leading one is implicit rather than stored in the fraction field. Special exponent patterns change this rule: zero exponents support zeros and subnormals, while all-one exponents support infinities and NaNs depending on the fraction. A NaN is a special value indicating a non-number result or state. Reading only the exponent field is therefore not enough to classify every value. The fields form one interpretation rule, not three independent ordinary integers.
actions: Classify the all-one exponent with zero and nonzero fraction fields separately.

question.prompt: Why does an all-one exponent not identify infinity by itself?
question.answer: A zero fraction indicates infinity, while a nonzero fraction indicates a NaN in the IEEE binary formats discussed here.

slides.title: Some decimal fractions are exactly binary fractions
keyPoints: The exact sum is 3/4
slides.narration: Not every floating-point operation is inexact. The first value is five eighths, which has the finite binary expansion zero point one zero one. The second is one eighth. Their sum is six eighths, or three quarters, which also fits exactly in binary. The program checks the binary radix assumption at compilation and prints first=0.625, sum=0.750, and exact three quarters=true. The three printed decimal places are a formatting choice; they do not create the exactness. The mathematical denominators being powers of two and the values fitting available precision explain it. Contrast this with one tenth, whose binary expansion repeats and needs rounding in a finite binary format.
actions: Express both inputs as fractions with denominator eight before Run.

slides.title: Equality is not a NaN detector
keyPoints: A NaN is unequal to itself
Use the classification operation
Validation can reject nonfinite measurements explicitly
slides.narration: The program creates a quiet NaN without performing an invalid memory operation or relying on input from a sensor. Its equality comparison with itself prints false. std::isnan recognizes the category and prints true. Our measurement contract accepts finite nonnegative values, so the NaN is rejected while zero is accepted. The output therefore distinguishes a legitimate zero reading from a special non-number state. A test such as value == NaN would not detect the category. The standard classification functions state the intent clearly. This example assumes quiet NaN support, checked at compilation, and ordinary floating-point semantics rather than compiler options that discard NaN behavior.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
keyPoints: Exact equality can be valid for this deliberate demonstration. It is usually a poor universal test for the results of different floating-point calculations.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Use a fixed epsilon as a universal rule for all magnitudes. A bound useful near 1 can be too tight or too loose elsewhere.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: State an error budget and test both near-zero and scaled values. Keep NaN handling explicit rather than letting an accidental comparison decide policy.

slides.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
keyPoints: An absolute tolerance gives a useful bound near zero; a relative tolerance scales with magnitude. The application chooses both from its error budget. Closeness is not a universal equivalence relation: it can fail transitivity, so it must not replace ordering in a sorted container. This lab covers modest finite magnitudes; a fully general comparator must also avoid overflow in difference and tolerance calculations.
A plausible alternative: Use integers for exact bounded counts; use floating point for a wide range of approximate measurements. This example assumes the normal nearest-even rounding mode.

slides.title: Floating-Point Concepts
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: The sign distinguishes positive and negative values.
In common IEEE 754 binary formats, it is stored separately from exponent and fraction fields.
Unlike two’s-complement integers, changing only the floating-point sign bit changes the sign of an ordinary finite value without changing its magnitude.
The format also contains positive and negative zero.
slides.narration: The sign distinguishes positive and negative values. In common IEEE 754 binary formats, it is stored separately from exponent and fraction fields. Unlike two’s-complement integers, changing only the floating-point sign bit changes the sign of an ordinary finite value without changing its magnitude. The format also contains positive and negative zero. They compare equal in ordinary numerical comparison, but operations such as reciprocal can distinguish them under IEEE arithmetic. A diagnostic that prints only 0 can therefore hide a representational distinction relevant to numerical algorithms or branch-cut conventions. The exponent determines the power-of-two scale. Normal binary floating-point values have the form (-1)^s * (1.f) * 2^e . The stored exponent is biased so the field can represent both negative and positive exponents without a separate exponent sign bit. For binary32, the exponent field has eight bits and the normal-value bias is 127. A stored exponent of 130 therefore corresponds to an exponent of 3. Some exponent field values are reserved for zero, subnormal values, infinity, and NaN, so not every field pattern describes an ordinary normalized scale. The significand carries the significant digits. For a normalized binary value, the leading digit is always one, so common IEEE binary formats omit that leading one from storage. Binary32 stores 23 fraction bits but has 24 bits of normal-value precision. Binary64 stores 52 fraction bits and has 53 bits of normal-value precision. Precision is the number of significant bits, not the number of fixed decimal places. A value near one and a value near one billion do not have the same absolute spacing between representable neighbors. Numerical error requirements should therefore distinguish absolute error from relative error. [ R9 ]

slides.narration: Start with the decimal value 13.25. The integer part 13 is binary 1101 ; the fraction 0.25 is 0.01 , so the complete binary value is 1101.01 . Normalize it to 1.10101 * 2^3 . The sign is zero. The stored exponent is 3 + 127 = 130 , or binary 10000010 . The stored fraction is 10101 followed by zeros to fill 23 positions. Its numeric field is 0x540000 . Combining sign, exponent, and fraction gives the 32-bit pattern 0x41540000 . This value is exactly representable because its binary expansion terminates within the available precision. Companion listing: ch05/float_bits.c The reference platform prints 0x41540000 . The numeric interpretation of a copied representation also assumes the reference platform’s compatible integer and float byte ordering; the format checks alone do not prove every representation detail on every machine. The example inspects a platform representation rather than defining a portable wire encoding. For a second trace, add 1 to binary32 16,777,216. The exact result lies halfway between 16,777,216 and 16,777,218. Under round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, it rounds to 16,777,216. The addition occurred, but the format could not retain that unit difference. This is precision loss, not integer-style wraparound.

slides.title: Rounding follows the spacing near the result
keyPoints: Representable values are not evenly spaced across all magnitudes
A unit can disappear at a large scale
A printed result may hide stored approximation
slides.narration: Near a large power of two, neighboring representable numbers can be farther apart than one. Adding one may then produce the same stored value under the selected rounding rule. That is precision loss, not integer wraparound and not proof that the processor skipped the addition. Near zero, the spacing is much smaller, so the same format retains much finer absolute detail. A short decimal display can conceal these differences by rounding for presentation again. When diagnosing a numerical issue, identify the input values, format, rounding assumptions, and required tolerance. Printing more digits can reveal evidence, but it does not restore information that the arithmetic already rounded away.
actions: Draw two nearby representable values with the exact result between them.

question.prompt: If a large floating value plus one compares equal to itself, must the addition have been skipped?
question.answer: No. The exact mathematical result may round back to the same representable value at that magnitude.

slides.title: An equality policy needs scale and special-value rules
keyPoints: Absolute tolerance helps near zero
Relative tolerance scales with magnitude
NaNs and infinities need explicit treatment
slides.narration: Suppose a sensor's accepted absolute error near zero is one billionth. A result of one ten-billionth may be close to zero even though relative error against zero is not useful. At a magnitude of one million, a relative tolerance of one millionth allows a difference of one. Whether that is acceptable depends on the measurement, not on a universal magic epsilon. A useful comparison can combine an absolute floor with a relative scale, then define behavior for infinities and NaNs separately. The chapter's helper validates tolerance inputs as well. That validation matters because a negative or non-number tolerance would make the intended acceptance rule unclear.
actions: Compare the two stated magnitudes and calculate the allowed differences.

question.prompt: Why is relative tolerance alone awkward when comparing a tiny result with zero?
question.answer: Scaling by the magnitude near zero can make the allowance vanish or become too small for the application’s absolute error budget.

slides.title: Changing evaluation order can change the stored answer
keyPoints: Floating addition need not be associative
Intermediate rounding affects later work
Reproducibility includes compiler and algorithm choices
slides.narration: In exact arithmetic, regrouping three additions does not change their sum. In finite floating-point arithmetic, each intermediate result may round. Combining a tiny value with a very large one can lose the tiny contribution before a later subtraction would have made it visible. Combining the large values first can leave a different result. Neither observation permits us to ignore the mathematical target; it tells us the chosen algorithm and order affect error. Compiler reassociation options can also change the intended sequence. For a reproducible study, keep the input set, order, format, build flags, and reference calculation clear. A timing comparison without those controls may compare different numerical computations.
actions: Ask learners where information can be lost before a later cancellation occurs.

question.prompt: Why must a summation experiment record optimization options as well as input values?
question.answer: Some options permit reassociation or other transformations that alter rounding order and numerical results.

slides.title: Avoid unnecessary intermediate overflow
keyPoints: A representable final result can have an overflowing naive intermediate
Use an algorithm designed for the numerical range
Wider types are not the only repair
slides.narration: To compute a distance, a naive expression squares two coordinates, adds the squares, and takes a square root. The squares can exceed the finite range even when the final distance would fit. A suitable hypot implementation uses scaling to avoid that unnecessary intermediate failure. This is a design lesson: changing every variable to a wider type may postpone a problem, while changing the algorithm can address its cause. Very small results have their own issues, including subnormal values and rounding to zero. Do not treat every tiny number as automatically invalid. Ask whether the remaining information meets the domain's error budget and whether a more stable formulation is available.

question.answer: The intermediate squares can exceed the finite range even when the final norm is representable.

slides.narration: Floating-point surprises are easier to manage when we replace the phrase computers are bad at decimals with a concrete explanation. One tenth has a repeating binary expansion, so the stored value is a nearby representable number. Arithmetic uses those stored inputs and rounds results under the active rules. Presentation may round the displayed digits again. None of this is random behavior. The engineering task is to choose a representation and algorithm whose error remains acceptable, then validate the exceptional states. Explain each numerical defect by locating the lost information or violated domain rule. That approach produces a repair more precise than adding an arbitrary tolerance everywhere.

example.title: A small value can disappear in a large sum
example.text:
const double large = 9007199254740992.0;
    const double sum = large + 1.0;
explain: This constant is 2 to the power 53. The preceding static_assert lines require the floating-point representation used by this demonstration at compile time.

At this magnitude, binary64 cannot represent every consecutive integer. Under the default round-to-nearest environment, adding one rounds back to large. Floating-point addition is not exact real-number addition.
example.invariant: The demonstration uses binary64 with the ordinary round-to-nearest environment. Decimal notation does not imply exact storage of every integer.
